evaluation.positioning_hook: A charming art thief breaks out of prison to steal Van Gogh’s Irises from the Getty, while the detective who put him away races to stop him and can’t quite stop loving him.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clean, easy-to-sell engine: a glamorous museum heist, a romantic adversary, and a comic crew with clear personalities. The Van Gogh/ Getty setting gives it upscale familiarity, while the prison-break-to-heist structure broadens the hook beyond a niche caper.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands immediately in the Getty opening and stays legible all the way through: Brax wants Irises, Roz wants him, and the museum is the battlefield. The script keeps the objective and the obstacle visible in almost every sequence.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Brax is a strong lead because he’s both a criminal mastermind and a romantic softie, and Roz has the right mix of competence, irritation, and vulnerability. The supporting crew—Vic, Charles, Lang, Serena, Jimmy Lee—each have enough flavor to make the ensemble pop.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s most distinctive move is turning a museum heist into a romantic chess match with art-history banter, elaborate gadgetry, and a prison-break alibi. The fake-Irises-room reveal and the grandma provenance turn give it a fresher identity than a standard caper.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The heist mechanics keep escalating cleanly: prison prep, museum infiltration, pipe access, camera hacks, false identities, and the final canyon escape. The script is built on reversals and timed reveals, so it keeps generating forward motion.

resonant_originality.reasoning: It feels like a familiar genre shape made specific by the Getty, the art-world provenance thread, and the ex-lovers-on-opposite-sides dynamic. The ending ties the caper to family history in a way that makes the theft feel emotionally motivated, not just procedural.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Getty security ecosystem, museum donor politics, prison logistics, and art provenance details create a world with real operational texture. It’s not a sprawling universe, but the script knows the rules of its spaces and uses them well.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is breezy, flirtatious, and self-aware without losing the mechanics of the caper. The banter between Brax, Roz, Vic, and Lang gives the script a distinct comic register that feels more playful than grim.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The provenance reveal and Roz’s family connection to the painting add a meaningful second layer beneath the heist. The script hints at bigger emotional stakes around art, inheritance, and atonement, even though the surface drive remains the caper.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Brax/Roz is the central engine, but the crew dynamics are strong enough that multiple pairings generate material: Vic/Ashley, Charles/Serena, Brax/Lang, Roz/Davis. The script repeatedly mines friction, loyalty, and flirtation across the ensemble.

lead_characters.name: Braxton Montgomery
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, polished, white-collar criminal with elite taste and a prison record.
lead_characters.hook: A dapper, hyper-competent art thief with the soul of a romantic and the instincts of a chess player. Brax is all charm, precision, and self-mythology, but the script keeps revealing that his biggest compulsion is emotional: he wants to atone, win Roz back, and prove he can be more than the crime he’s known for.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of George Clooney in Ocean’s Eleven — effortless charisma, comic timing, and the ability to make criminal behavior feel seductive. It also gives an actor the rare chance to play a suave mastermind who is secretly wounded, funny, and genuinely vulnerable.

lead_characters.name: Roz Reno
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-40s, law enforcement, sharp, physically capable, emotionally guarded.
lead_characters.hook: A relentless investigator who can outthink a room and outfight most of it, but can’t fully shut down the emotional damage Brax left behind. Roz is funny because she’s unsentimental, compelling because she’s not cold, and structurally vital because she’s the only person who can truly read Brax in real time.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Sandra Bullock in The Heat — a tough, fast-talking law-enforcement lead who can carry action, comedy, and romantic tension at once. It gives an actor the chance to play authority without stiffness and heartbreak without melodrama.

lead_characters.name: Victor
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, married, tech-savvy, socially frazzled, comic supporting player.
lead_characters.hook: Brax’s camera-hacking, gadget-building right hand, who talks like he’s always one domestic complaint away from a breakdown. Vic is the kind of supporting character who makes the heist feel lived-in: funny, needy, loyal, and just insecure enough to be dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Don Cheadle in Ocean’s Eleven — a fast, specific ensemble operator who gets to be both comic relief and indispensable machinery. The role rewards an actor who can make tech exposition feel like personality.

lead_characters.name: Charles
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s-30s, hearing-impaired, fluent in ASL, nimble and observant.
lead_characters.hook: A quiet, hyper-precise thief whose stillness becomes one of the crew’s most useful weapons. Charles is the stealth MVP of the movie, and the script gives him a real personality beyond function: dry, romantic, competitive, and unexpectedly funny.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Daniel Dae Kim in Lost or a strong silent ensemble player in a heist film — a role built on physical intelligence, timing, and expressive restraint. It gives an actor the chance to dominate scenes without needing volume.

lead_characters.name: Lang
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, intimidating, muscular, tattooed, criminal associate.
lead_characters.hook: A volatile, swaggering enforcer who keeps trying to turn every plan into a power play. Lang is the crew’s pressure valve and wildcard, a guy whose menace is always undercut by the fact that he’s also funny, petty, and weirdly needy for respect.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Walton Goggins in a crime ensemble — a role that lets an actor weaponize charm, threat, and comic irritation in the same scene. It’s a juicy antagonist-supporting part with real scene-stealing potential.

lead_characters.name: Serena
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, athletic, glamorous, physically capable, Olympic-level background.
lead_characters.hook: A lethal distraction with real athletic credibility, Serena is more than eye candy: she’s disciplined, competitive, and fully capable of carrying the physical side of the plan. The script uses her as both a tactical asset and a romantic/comic presence, which gives her a strong, modern utility.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Gina Carano in Haywire — a physically commanding role that still wants charisma and wit. It gives an actor a chance to sell competence first and glamour second.

lead_characters.name: Jimmy Lee
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s-30s, decorated ex-military sniper, socially awkward, intense.
lead_characters.hook: A dead-serious marksman with a bizarrely earnest romantic streak and a gift for absurdly precise violence. Jimmy Lee is the kind of supporting character who can be both the straight man and the surprise comic engine, which makes him memorable fast.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Shannon in a lighter ensemble mode — a role where deadpan intensity becomes comedy and competence becomes character. It gives an actor a chance to play lethal, awkward, and oddly sweet all at once.

lead_characters.name: Dale Davis
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s-50s, head of security, arrogant, tech-forward, status-conscious.
lead_characters.hook: The smug security chief whose confidence is so inflated it becomes part of the heist’s fun. Davis is a great obstacle because he’s not stupid; he’s just so convinced his system is unbeatable that he practically invites the takedown.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Giamatti in a prestige-comic authority role — a character who gets to be pompous, funny, and humiliated without ever becoming a cartoon. It’s a delicious antagonist-supporting part.

lead_characters.name: Ashley
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, Vic’s spouse, offscreen for much of the film, emotionally grounded.
lead_characters.hook: The unseen domestic reality that keeps puncturing Vic’s self-importance. Ashley is a smart supporting presence because the script uses him to humanize Vic and give the movie a surprising, modern relationship texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that benefits from a strong character actor cameo — the showcase is specificity, not page count. It gives an actor a sharp, memorable domestic counterpoint in a crime comedy.

lead_characters.name: Grandma
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 80s, elderly, frail but mentally sharp, family matriarch.
lead_characters.hook: Roz’s grandmother is the emotional vault of the movie, holding the family history that recontextualizes the entire heist. She starts as a sweet comic elder and ends up as the keeper of the painting’s true home, which gives the finale real emotional lift.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of June Squibb in Nebraska — a role where warmth, wit, and hidden authority all matter. It gives an older actor a late-film reveal with real emotional payoff.

casting_characteristics: one physically imposing tattooed male role

notable_requirements: Getty Center museum interiors and exteriors

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical illusion work, camera-feed manipulation, drone rigging, and a few explosion/lockdown beats; no heavy creature or digital-world requirements.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, explosions, pepper spray, zipline work, rooftop movement, fight beats, water-in-pipe sequence, and practical security-system effects.

rights_flags.detail: Vincent van Gogh's Irises and other named artworks referenced throughout

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: theatrical or streamer-premiere caper with broad adult appeal

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly interior, but the Getty set pieces, rooftop work, prison break, drone rig, zipline finale, and multiple night exteriors push this above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Brax and Roz need strong chemistry, Charles requires a hearing-impaired performer comfortable with ASL, and the ensemble only works if the supporting crew each lands as a distinct comic type.

development.note: The heist mechanics are clear, but the script is carrying a lot of moving parts: romance, art-history provenance, prison logistics, and ensemble comedy all have to stay in balance.

comp_set.title: Ocean's Eleven
comp_set.why_it_comps: The polished ensemble caper energy, luxury setting, and pleasure of watching a smart crew outmaneuver security are directly in this lane.

comp_set.title: The Thomas Crown Affair
comp_set.why_it_comps: The cat-and-mouse romance between thief and investigator, plus the upscale art-world backdrop, is the script’s clearest tonal cousin.

comp_set.title: Logan Lucky
comp_set.why_it_comps: The blue-collar-to-clever-heist mechanics and the comic crew dynamics echo the same audience pleasure of watching a plan unfold with personality.

comp_set.title: Now You See Me
comp_set.why_it_comps: The elaborate misdirection, timed reveals, and showy set-piece construction fit the same audience appetite for spectacle-driven caper mechanics.

comp_set.title: The Italian Job
comp_set.why_it_comps: The team-based theft, vehicle movement, and clean, crowd-pleasing momentum align with this script’s final-act escape energy.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like stylish heist movies with romance, banter, and a clean puzzle-box payoff.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but very accessible to women through the Brax/Roz relationship; mainstream streamer and theatrical specialty audience.

budget_tier.note: The Getty locations, night exteriors, prison material, stunt work, and ensemble cast point to a polished mid-budget caper rather than a lean indie.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals execs building adult four-quadrant genre
producer-financed caper packages with star attachment upside
director-driven genre labels looking for a glossy crowd-pleaser
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the glossy adult caper lane: smart, accessible, and built around a star-friendly lead role plus a strong female counterweight. The museum setting and art-world stakes make it feel premium without requiring franchise scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. Brax and Roz have sequel-friendly chemistry, but the story resolves its central heist and emotional arc cleanly, and no separate universe or spin-off vector is materially set up.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Getty is a great heist arena.
strengths.what_it_means: The museum setting gives the movie instant prestige texture and a built-in obstacle course of security, sightlines, and public scrutiny. That makes the project easier to pitch to buyers who want a recognizable, upscale world without needing a period budget.
strengths.evidence: The opening Getty walkthrough, the security command center, the roof access, the pipe route, and the final gala all turn the museum into a playable machine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Brax and Roz are a real engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The script has a built-in romantic cat-and-mouse dynamic that can sell the movie even before the heist mechanics are explained. That is exactly the kind of chemistry-dependent hook that attracts actors and gives marketing a clean emotional spine.
strengths.evidence: Their first museum exchange, the prison interview, the repeated near-kisses, and the final confrontation on the cliff all keep the relationship active.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble is functional and funny.
strengths.what_it_means: Each crew member has a distinct utility and comic voice, which makes the heist feel collaborative rather than generic. That broadens casting appeal and gives the movie multiple scene-stealing opportunities.
strengths.evidence: Vic’s tech obsession, Charles’ ASL precision, Lang’s volatility, Serena’s athletic distraction, and Jimmy Lee’s sniper deadpan all play as separate flavors.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The provenance reveal adds emotional weight.
strengths.what_it_means: The art theft is not just about money; it becomes about family history, restitution, and what “home” means for a stolen object. That gives the movie a more premium finish and a reason for the audience to care beyond the mechanics.
strengths.evidence: Roz discovering Klimasz Incorporated, Grandma’s story about Warsaw, and the final return of Irises to her wall.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The set-piece design is very clean.
strengths.what_it_means: The script keeps building visual problems that are easy to understand and fun to watch solve, which is a major commercial asset in a caper. Buyers can see the trailer in the writing: disguise, infiltration, misdirection, and a big final escape.
strengths.evidence: The chroma-suit infiltration, the bathroom stall sequence, the fake-Irises room, and the zipline getaway.

whats_special.headline: This is a polished, star-friendly caper with a real romantic hook and a museum setting that feels premium without becoming unmakeable. The script’s strongest commercial advantage is that it pairs a clean heist engine with a relationship buyers can sell in one sentence, while the ensemble and provenance twist give it enough texture to stand out in a crowded genre lane.

items.area: The script is carrying a lot of moving parts.
items.detail: The movie has to juggle prison logistics, museum security, romance, ensemble comedy, art-history provenance, and a double-heist structure. That’s not a deal-breaker, but it does make the project more conditional on execution than the clean premise suggests.

items.area: Brax’s plan depends on a lot of coincidence.
items.detail: The fake marshal call, the burner-phone swap, the hidden replica, the pipe access, and the exact timing of the security resets all stack up into a very engineered finale. Buyers will clock that the movie is more elaborate than casual, which narrows the lane to audiences who like puzzle-box capers.

items.area: The romance can crowd the heist.
items.detail: Brax and Roz are the movie’s biggest asset, but their emotional back-and-forth also risks pulling attention away from the theft mechanics in the middle stretch. That’s a real balancing act for a buyer because the script is strongest when both engines are moving together.

items.area: The supporting crew is vivid, but still functional.
items.detail: Vic, Charles, Lang, Serena, and Jimmy Lee all pop, but most of them are defined by what they do for the plan rather than by deep independent arcs. That keeps the movie lean, but it also means the ensemble is more of a strong support system than a franchise-level bench.

items.area: The clearance list is not trivial.
items.detail: The script names the Getty Center, LAPD, FBI, U.S. Marshals, Apple Watch, Ikea, Postmates, Lloyd’s of London, Paw Patrol, El Torito, Trader Joe’s, and multiple real artworks and artists including Van Gogh, Monet, Picasso, Rivera, Pollock, Klee, Chardin, and Géricault. That’s manageable for development, but it is a real legal and business-affairs pass before greenlight.

issues.headline: The movie’s biggest strength is also its biggest pressure point: it’s a very busy caper, and the audience has to track a lot of moving machinery while still buying the romance. The other conversation buyers will have is clearance and scope — not because it’s impossible, but because the script is built out of enough named institutions, brands, and artworks that the legal pass matters.
